title: Application deployment
intro: Deploy to your own server with PM2 or Docker, or deploy to NocoBase Studio. Choose a method and use an Agent or follow the manual steps.
copyFailed: Copy failed. Select and copy the text manually.

guides.label: PM2
guides.title: Deploy an application with PM2
guides.description: Build an archive locally, install and update it over SSH with app-installer, and let PM2 manage the application process.

blocks.text: Install Node.js 24+ and pnpm locally, and configure SSH access. Install Node.js 24 and tar on the Linux server, then install PM2 (4.3+) as the deployment account:

blocks.code: npm install --global pm2

blocks.text: Make sure non-interactive SSH sessions can find node and pm2. The deployment account must be able to write to the installation directory and its parent; use a new or empty directory for the first installation.

blocks.code:
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build --target linux-x64 --node-version 24 --tar

blocks.text: The archive is written to storage/exports/dist.tar.gz. Supply the initial administrator password through the local INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variable, then install:

blocks.code:
npx --yes @nocobase/app-installer@beta install \
  --ssh deploy@server.example.com \
  --dir /srv/apps/purchase \
  --archive storage/exports/dist.tar.gz \
  --origin https://purchase.example.com \
  --base-path /main \
  --port 13000 --name nocobase-purchase \
  --set-from-env users.initialAdmin.password=INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD \
  --json

blocks.text: The installer uploads the archive, generates configuration, runs migrations, and starts the application. These examples use @beta; pin a tested installer version in CI.

blocks.code: pm2 startup

blocks.text: Run the system service command printed by PM2, then save the process list as the same deployment account:

blocks.code: pm2 save

blocks.text: After configuring HTTPS and the reverse proxy described above, check application status and public access:

blocks.code:
npx --yes @nocobase/app-installer@beta status \
  --ssh deploy@server.example.com \
  --dir /srv/apps/purchase --json

curl --fail --silent --show-error \
  https://purchase.example.com/main/api/healthz

blocks.text: Confirm that status reports result.health.ok as true and result.pending as null, and that the health endpoint returns ok: true. Open the application and verify sign-in.
Rebuild the archive, check status for unfinished operations, then run the upgrade preflight:

blocks.code:
npx --yes @nocobase/app-installer@beta upgrade \
  --ssh deploy@server.example.com \
  --dir /srv/apps/purchase \
  --archive storage/exports/dist.tar.gz \
  --json

blocks.text: Review the preflight result, downtime, and backup plan, then repeat the command with --yes to apply the update. Repeat the status and access checks afterward. The installer backs up SQLite and configuration; back up uploads separately. For an external database, back it up first and add --backup-done.

skill.title: Use an Agent for PM2 deployment

blocks.text: Install the nocobase-app-installer Skill, start a new Agent session in the application directory, and send the prompt below. Use this Skill for external databases, rollback, and CI/CD as well.

blocks.code: npx skills@latest add nocobase/skills-v3 --skill nocobase-app-installer -g

Use the nocobase-app-installer Skill to deploy this application with PM2.
SSH: deploy@server.example.com
Directory: /srv/apps/purchase
Public URL: https://purchase.example.com/main
Database: SQLite
Check the environment and configuration, then deploy and verify.

guides.label: Docker
guides.title: Deploy an application with Docker
guides.description: Build an image with the Dockerfile included in your application, then run it on the server with configuration and data mounted. Install Docker on both machines and sign in to your image registry.

sections.title: 1. Build and distribute the Docker image

blocks.code:
docker build --platform linux/amd64 \
  -t registry.example.com/purchase:release-001 .
docker push registry.example.com/purchase:release-001

blocks.text: The Dockerfile installs dependencies and builds the application; no prior pnpm build is needed. Keep Dockerfile.dockerignore alongside it to exclude configuration, secrets, and data. This example targets x64; use linux/arm64 for an ARM64 server.

blocks.code: docker pull registry.example.com/purchase:release-001

blocks.text: For the first deployment, create dedicated directories and generate a SQLite configuration with unique secrets. The container runs as UID 1000 and needs read and write access to these directories.

blocks.code:
sudo install -d -o 1000 -g 1000 -m 750 \
  /srv/apps/purchase /srv/apps/purchase/storage

docker run --rm \
  --mount type=bind,src=/srv/apps/purchase,dst=/config \
  registry.example.com/purchase:release-001 \
  node dist/cli/index.js config init \
  --config /config/config.yml --dialect sqlite

blocks.text: Supply the initial administrator password through the server’s INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variable, then write it to the configuration:

blocks.code:
docker run --rm -e INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD \
  --mount type=bind,src=/srv/apps/purchase/config.yml,dst=/app/config.yml \
  registry.example.com/purchase:release-001 \
  node dist/cli/index.js config set --from-env \
  users.initialAdmin.password=INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD

blocks.text: Keep config.yml and storage/ on the host and reuse them across image updates. The project’s .env is not passed to the container automatically; supply any additional variables with the same -e or --env-file options for configuration checks and startup.

sections.title: 3. Start and verify the Docker container

blocks.text: Check the configuration, then start the container after the check passes:

blocks.code:
docker run --rm \
  -v /srv/apps/purchase/config.yml:/app/config.yml:ro \
  -v /srv/apps/purchase/storage:/app/storage \
  registry.example.com/purchase:release-001 \
  node dist/cli/index.js config check

docker run -d --name purchase \
  --init --restart unless-stopped --stop-timeout 60 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:13000:13000 \
  -e APP_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=https://purchase.example.com \
  -e APP_BASE_PATH=/main \
  -v /srv/apps/purchase/config.yml:/app/config.yml:ro \
  -v /srv/apps/purchase/storage:/app/storage \
  registry.example.com/purchase:release-001

blocks.text: After configuring HTTPS and the reverse proxy described above, check the container and public access:

blocks.code:
docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' purchase

curl --fail --silent --show-error \
  https://purchase.example.com/main/api/healthz

blocks.text: Wait for the container to become healthy, confirm that the health endpoint returns ok: true, and verify sign-in in the application. To investigate failures, run docker logs --tail 100 purchase.
Rebuild and push with a new tag, such as release-002, keeping the old image. Pull the new image, repeat the configuration check with its tag, and stop the old container only after the check passes:

blocks.code: docker pull registry.example.com/purchase:release-002
docker stop --timeout 60 purchase

blocks.text: While the application is stopped, back up config.yml, storage/, and any external database. After confirming the backup, remove the old container:

blocks.code: docker rm purchase

blocks.text: Repeat the start command with release-002, keeping the same configuration, data mounts, and environment variables, then repeat the checks. Restarting a container does not update its image. Docker does not back up data automatically; check database compatibility before reverting to an older image.

skill.title: Use an Agent for Docker deployment

blocks.text: The application already includes the nocobase-deployment Skill. Ask an Agent to use it from the project directory, including for multi-platform builds, offline distribution, and CI/CD.

blocks.code:
Use the nocobase-deployment Skill to deploy this application with Docker.
SSH: deploy@server.example.com
Image: registry.example.com/purchase:release-001
Directory: /srv/apps/purchase
Public URL: https://purchase.example.com/main
Database: SQLite
Check the configuration and data mounts, then deploy and verify.

guides.label: NocoBase Studio
guides.title: Deploy to NocoBase Studio
guides.description: Deploy your local application to an existing NocoBase Studio instance: install the CLI, sign in, select the application, build locally, then upload, deploy, and verify with nb-studio. This example uses an in-process environment that accepts archives and an application already associated with its source repository in Studio.

skill.title: Deploy to Studio with an Agent

blocks.text: For first-time setup, sign in to the target Studio instance, open Use Studio in your agent from the avatar menu, and send the complete setup instructions to your local coding agent. It installs the CLI and guides you through checking the verification code and approving sign-in in your browser. You can also prepare the CLI manually using the steps below.

Once connected, send the request below from your application project directory using your actual signed-in profile, application, and environment. The agent checks the application’s associated repository and commit, builds locally, then uploads, deploys, and verifies with nb-studio.

blocks.context: Send to your local coding agent
blocks.code:
Use the nb-studio CLI to help me deploy this application to Studio.
Studio URL: https://studio.example.com/studio
CLI profile: studio
Application ID: purchase
Environment ID: preview

Check the CLI identity, application, and deployment environment first.
Create the application if it does not exist.
Confirm that Studio can determine the source repository from the target application, the changes are committed and pushed, and the working tree is clean.
Record the full commit SHA and build storage/exports/dist.tar.gz for the target platform.
Upload with release upload, passing --app, --sha, and --file explicitly.
Take the release ID from result.data.release.id.
Check required variables and resolve missing values before deployment.
Use app deploy for that release, or request deployment if protected.
Check deployment status, application status, error logs, access, and sign-in.
Return the application URL, release ID, and verification results.
Clearly state when approval is still pending.

blocks.text: Run the following commands in a Bash terminal on your local computer, using macOS, Linux, or Windows WSL. Sign in to the target Studio instance in your browser. Open Use Studio in your agent from the avatar menu, copy the CLI installation command from the setup instructions, and run it locally. The command includes a download token valid for 30 minutes; generate a new one if it expires. The example below shows the format only. Use the complete command generated by your Studio instance:

blocks.code:
curl -fsSL https://studio.example.com/studio/api/agents/dist/installScript \
  | sh -s -- --token '<download-token>'

blocks.text: Studio supplies nb-studio; it is not installed with npm install -g @nocobase/studio-cli. One CLI installation can connect to several Studio instances. By default, the command is in ~/.local/bin. Add it to the current terminal’s PATH and check the installation:

blocks.code:
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
nb-studio --version

blocks.text: If a new terminal cannot find nb-studio, add the PATH setting above to your shell’s startup file.

This example uses the studio profile. Replace the server URL and profile directly in the commands. The Studio URL must include its deployment path, such as /studio. A profile is the local name for this instance; use a different profile for each instance.

blocks.code:
nb-studio --profile studio login \
  --server https://studio.example.com/studio
nb-studio --profile studio whoami --json

blocks.text: login displays a sign-in URL and verification code. Open the URL, check and approve the code in your browser, then use whoami to confirm the instance, identity, and permissions.
This example uses the purchase application and preview environment. Replace them with your application and environment IDs. Start by checking the available environments and target application:

blocks.code:
nb-studio --profile studio env list --json
nb-studio --profile studio app get purchase --json

blocks.text: Confirm that the target environment accepts archives and that your account can view, upload, configure, deploy, and read application logs. Only if the application does not exist, create it using an ID from the environment list:

blocks.code:
nb-studio --profile studio app create purchase \
  --name "Purchase" --env preview --json

blocks.text: In this example, Studio determines the source repository from the target application. Confirm that the application is associated with its repository in Studio and that Studio can access it to verify commits. Newly created applications also need this association.

From the application project root, confirm that the changes to deploy are committed and pushed. git status --short should produce no output. Record the full commit SHA returned by git rev-parse HEAD, then install dependencies and build. This example targets Linux x64 with Node.js 24. Adjust these options if the Studio environment uses a different platform or Node.js version.

blocks.code:
git status --short
git rev-parse HEAD

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build --target linux-x64 --node-version 24 --tar

blocks.text: The archive is generated at storage/exports/dist.tar.gz and contains code, production dependencies, and a configuration template. Migrate your local database, uploaded files, and other business data separately.

Use nb-studio release upload with your signed-in profile to upload the archive. Studio uses the repository associated with the target application. Replace the placeholder after --sha with the full commit SHA used for the build above. The commit must be pushed to the remote repository and verifiable by Studio.

blocks.code:
nb-studio --profile studio release upload \
  --app purchase \
  --sha '<commit-sha>' \
  --file storage/exports/dist.tar.gz \
  --json

blocks.text: The CLI obtains an upload ticket and uploads the file automatically. After success, take the release ID from result.data.release.id in the JSON response and use it in the next step. Uploading alone does not start the application. If release is null or superseded is true, a newer commit has superseded the build; build and upload again.
To check the uploaded release, list the application’s releases:

blocks.code: nb-studio --profile studio release list purchase --json

blocks.text: In each command below, replace the placeholder after --release with the release ID you identified above. Check its required variables first. If any report missing: true, set them in the application’s Variables tab in Studio before deploying:

blocks.code:
nb-studio --profile studio app env list purchase \
  --release '<release-id>' --json

blocks.text: For an unprotected environment, run this command to deploy the release you just uploaded:

blocks.code:
nb-studio --profile studio app deploy purchase \
  --release '<release-id>' \
  --wait true --json

blocks.text: --wait true waits for up to about 100 seconds. If the response still shows queued or deploying, continue checking its status. For a protected environment, use the request command below and wait for an approver to authorize deployment:

blocks.code:
nb-studio --profile studio deploy request purchase \
  --release '<release-id>' --json

nb-studio --profile studio app get purchase --json
nb-studio --profile studio deploy list purchase --limit 5 --json
nb-studio --profile studio app logs purchase --level error --json

blocks.text: Confirm that this deployment has status succeeded, and check the application’s currentVersion and runtime.state. Open result.data.url from app get and verify the page, sign-in, and main workflows. If Studio generated initial administrator credentials, view and save them under Initial administrator on the application’s Overview tab.

If deployment fails, inspect its deployment logs in Studio. app logs reads application runtime logs. An empty error log does not establish success; also check deployment status and access the application.

Back up the database and uploaded files before updating. Commit and push the code changes, then build and upload the new commit. Deploy using the release ID returned by this upload and repeat verification. To apply variable changes alone, redeploy the current release. Code changes require a new archive.

When deploying to several Studio instances, set each instance’s address and profile, then upload, deploy, and verify separately. Release IDs belong to the instance receiving the upload and cannot be reused on another instance. Sign in again with the new URL if a Studio address changes.

environment.title: PM2 / Docker example environment and access
environment.description: The PM2 and Docker guides use the examples below. Replace the server, deployment directory, and public URL with your own before running the commands. Studio deployments use an environment configured by an administrator and the URL shown on the target App page.
accessSteps: Point purchase.example.com to the target server and configure a TLS certificate for HTTPS.
Configure a reverse proxy on the same server, forwarding to 127.0.0.1:13000 and preserving the /main path.
Enable WebSocket support and forward the public host and protocol to the application.
environment.note: The deployment commands below do not configure DNS, certificates, or a reverse proxy. Complete these settings before verifying public access.
